forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Tamworth took out no new loans in 2025/26 despite £17.2m of capital spending
news_drafts.lead:
Tamworth Borough Council took out no new loans in 2025/26, even though it spent £17.2m on capital spending (money spent on things that last, such as buildings and equipment). The figure is in the annual treasury management report (how the council borrows and invests its cash) that went to its Audit and Governance Committee on 24 September 2026.

The council's total borrowing stayed at £63.060m, unchanged from the year before. The report says the spending was paid for from the council's own cash and from capital receipts (money from asset sales), a practice known as internal borrowing. This saves interest but uses up the council's cash cushion. The report puts the gap between what the council has borrowed and what its capital spending would otherwise require at £7.158m, which it describes as an under-borrowed position.

The council says the reason was cost. In the report's words: "Due to the elevated cost of borrowing long-term, no borrowing was undertaken during the year." The papers describe the approach as a continuing strategy, not a one-year decision.

findings.committee: Prosperity, Place and Environment Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: LCTR scheme costs £5.6m, with 74% borne by County Council, 26% split between borough, police and fire
findings.detail: Current scheme cost is £5.6m as of October 2026, all borne by the Collection Fund but shared: County Council 74%, Borough Council 9%, Police & Crime Commissioner 13%, Fire & Rescue 4%. Costs have remained stable and accurate.
findings.matters: Shows Collection Fund pressure is managed through cost-sharing; limits borough's exposure and signals stable financial planning for vulnerable household support.
findings.figures: £5.6m total cost; 9% / 74% / 13% / 4% distribution across precepting authorities
findings.quote: The current cost is £5.6 m which is borne by the Council's Collection Fund, costs are shared between the Council and the Major Precepting Authorities in the following proportions. Borough Council (9%); County Council (74%); Police and Crime Commissioner (13%); Fire and Rescue Service (4%)

findings.committee: Prosperity, Place and Environment Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Estimated annual administrative savings of £10,000 to £14,000 from reduced LCTR correspondence
findings.detail: The 6,776 reduction in annual LCTR-related documents (bills, notices, reminders, summonses) translates to avoided printing, postage, fulfillment, processing and handling costs estimated at £10k-£14k per year.
findings.matters: Quantifies the operational savings from administrative simplification, providing business case evidence for banding schemes.
findings.figures: 6,776 avoided documents annually; estimated saving £10,000-£14,000 per year at £1.50-£2.00 per avoided item
findings.quote: A reasonable central estimate is therefore approximately £10,000 to £14,000 a year, based on an average combined cost of £1.50 to £2.00 per avoided item.

findings.committee: Prosperity, Place and Environment Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Government guidance mandates single harmonised working-age support scheme by Year 3 post-LGR
findings.detail: If Tamworth undergoes local government reorganisation, government guidance requires adoption of a unified working-age LCTR scheme across the new authority within three years.
findings.matters: Creates a future administrative and governance constraint; any council subject to LGR will need to plan for scheme harmonisation and potentially substantial integration work.
findings.quote: Government guidance for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) specifies that a single, harmonised working-age support scheme is mandatory across the new area by Year 3 at the latest.

findings.committee: Prosperity, Place and Environment Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Collection from LCTR accounts improved to 89.7% in 2024-25 from 86.0% in 2022-23
findings.detail: Post-banding implementation, collection rates from LCTR recipients improved by 3.7 percentage points. The council attributes this to the simplified, stable billing approach, which reduces disruption from frequent recalculation.
findings.matters: Demonstrates banding can improve credit discipline among vulnerable populations and reduce Collection Fund pressure—useful evidence for councils with collection challenges.
findings.quote: While collection of Council Tax from LCTR recipients is poorer than the overall figure, this is further confirmation that the banded scheme has contributed to better collection of LCTR debt.

findings.committee: Prosperity, Place and Environment Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: LCTR bills and adjustment correspondence fell 63.5% while working-age caseload rose 1.1%
findings.detail: After introducing the banded scheme in April 2024, LCTR-specific bills and adjustments fell from 9,999 to 3,649 annually, while the working-age caseload actually grew from 2,838 to 2,868. This demonstrates the scheme reduced routine administrative recalculation activity without restricting access to support.
findings.matters: Shows process simplification through banding can substantially reduce administrative burden while maintaining claimant access—directly relevant for other councils managing CTR pressures.
findings.figures: LCTR bills/adjustments down 63.5% (9,999 to 3,649); working-age caseload up 1.1% (2,838 to 2,868)
findings.quote: LCTR bills and adjustments fell from 9,999 to 3,649 a year, a reduction of 6,350 (63.5%)
